Clinical Reference

Sickle Cell Vaso-occlusive Crisis

On this page
A vaso-occlusive crisis (VOC) is an acute episode of ischemic pain caused by sickled red cells jamming the microcirculation — the defining event of sickle cell disease and the #1 reason these patients reach the ED. Treat pain fast, hunt for acute chest syndrome, and never mistake a pain crisis for drug-seeking.
HbSS / HbSβ⁰ = most severe Opioid within 30–60 min of arrival Acute chest syndrome = #1 cause of death Fever in SCD = emergency (asplenia) Hydroxyurea = first-line disease modifier
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — one letter, a whole disease

Sickle cell disease starts from a single point mutation in the β-globin gene — adenine→thymine (GAG→GTG) swaps glutamic acid for valine at position 6 of the β-chain, producing hemoglobin S (HbS). That one hydrophobic valine is a sticky patch. When HbS gives up its oxygen (deoxygenation), the exposed valine on one molecule latches onto a complementary pocket on the next, and HbS polymerizes into long rigid fibers that warp the soft biconcave red cell into a stiff, crescent (“sickle”) shape.

Early sickling is reversible with re-oxygenation, but each cycle damages the membrane. After enough cycles the cell becomes irreversibly sickled, dehydrated, and rigid. Two disasters follow, and they feed each other:

  • Hemolysis — fragile sickled cells lyse (average survival ~10–20 days vs 120). Chronic anemia results, and cell-free hemoglobin scavenges nitric oxide (NO) → vasoconstriction, endothelial activation, and over years pulmonary hypertension.
  • Vaso-occlusion — rigid sickled cells, now decorated with adhesion molecules, stick to activated endothelium (via P-selectin, VCAM-1) and to each other, recruiting neutrophils and platelets. The clog dams the post-capillary venule → downstream tissue ischemia → reperfusion injury and a burst of inflammation. That ischemic, inflamed tissue is what hurts: the vaso-occlusive crisis.

Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) cannot enter the HbS polymer, so it physically interrupts fiber growth. The more HbF a red cell carries, the harder it is to sickle — which is exactly why raising HbF is the master switch of therapy.

Deoxygenated HbS is like liquid soap that suddenly crystallizes into stiff needles when it cools. In the lungs (oxygen-rich, warm) it stays liquid and the cell is soft and slips through capillaries. Out in a cold, acidic, sluggish tissue bed it "sets" into needles that spear the cell into a crescent — and crescents pile up like logs jamming a river. Hydroxyurea keeps more of the "won't-crystallize" fetal form around; hydration and oxygen keep the soap liquid; crizanlizumab greases the vessel wall so the logs don't snag.
The vaso-occlusion cascade. Every therapy in this guide interrupts one labeled step — that is the through-line of the whole disease.
Peripheral smear: rigid, crescent-shaped sickled cells among normal biconcave RBCs — the morphologic signature of HbS polymerization.
Image: SpicyMilkBoy, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Normal red cell (A) vs sickle cell (B). Sickled cells occlude the small vessel (bottom), the mechanical basis of the crisis.
Image: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
Vaso-occlusion up close: rigid sickled cells adhere and pile up, damming the microcirculation and infarcting the tissue downstream.
Image: Kep17, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Read the whole guide through the cascade above. Hydroxyurea, transfusion and gene therapy stop the polymer from forming (raise HbF or lower HbS%). Hydration, oxygen, warmth and treating infection remove the deoxygenation trigger. L-glutamine shores up the red-cell membrane against oxidative injury. Crizanlizumab blocks the P-selectin adhesion that starts the clog. Opioids and NSAIDs do not touch the sickling at all — they treat the ischemic pain while the disease-modifying drugs and the body clear the occlusion.
🗂️

Genotypes & the acute crises — the vocabulary you'll use on rounds

By genotype (severity roughly tracks how much HbS a cell makes)

GenotypeBaseline severityTypical picture
HbSS (sickle cell anemia)Most severeLowest Hb (~6–9), most VOCs/ACS/stroke; ~60–70% of US SCD.
HbSβ⁰-thalassemiaSevere (≈ SS)No normal β-chain made → behaves like HbSS clinically.
HbSC diseaseIntermediateHigher Hb, more retinopathy & avascular necrosis; ACS still occurs.
HbSβ⁺-thalassemiaMild–moderateSome normal β-chain; severity varies with residual HbA.
Sickle cell trait (HbAS)CarrierNot a disease; rare exertional/altitude events, renal papillary necrosis, hematuria.

The acute crises — don't lump them all as "pain"

CrisisWhat defines itThe tell
Vaso-occlusive (pain) crisisIschemic pain — back, chest, extremities, abdomen; dactylitis in infants.Most common; the patient's typical pain with no better explanation.
Acute chest syndrome (ACS)New pulmonary infiltrate + fever and/or respiratory symptom/hypoxia/chest pain.Leading cause of death; can evolve during a VOC admission.
Splenic sequestrationSudden pooling of blood in spleen → big tender spleen + falling Hb + high retic.Young children; hypovolemic shock risk — transfuse.
Aplastic crisisAbrupt Hb drop with low reticulocytes.Parvovirus B19 shuts down marrow; retic count <1% is the clue.
Hyperhemolytic / hepaticRapid hemolysis or hepatic sequestration; jaundice, RUQ pain.Consider delayed transfusion reaction if recently transfused.
PriapismIschemic, painful erection >4 h.Urologic emergency; aspiration/phenylephrine irrigation.
When the Hb suddenly falls, the reticulocyte count sorts the emergency: high retic → the marrow is compensating, so cells are being lost peripherally (sequestration or hyperhemolysis); low retic → the marrow itself has stopped (aplastic crisis, think parvovirus B19).
Shared

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs of an acute VOC — frequency and the mechanism behind each

Frequencies are approximate for adults/adolescents presenting with an acute crisis (they vary with genotype and study). Read each finding as a clue to which vascular bed is occluded and whether a complication is brewing.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Acute pain (back, limbs, chest, abdomen)~95%The defining feature — ischemia of bone marrow and soft tissue from microvascular occlusion; marrow is a common site because of its sluggish sinusoidal flow.
Pain like the patient's prior crises~90%Recurrent occlusion of the same beds; a crisis that feels "different" should prompt a hunt for a complication (ACS, infection, AVN, cord).
Tachycardia / focal tenderness~50–70%Pain, stress and anemia drive sympathetic tone; local ischemic inflammation causes point tenderness/warmth.
Low-grade fever~40–60%Ischemia–reperfusion releases inflammatory cytokines; but never assume fever is "just the crisis" — asplenia makes infection deadly.
Dactylitis (hand–foot swelling)~20–30% (infants)Infarction of the small tubular bones of hands/feet; often the first VOC, age 6 months–2 years.
Dyspnea / hypoxia / new chest pain~15–20%Red flag for acute chest syndrome — pulmonary vaso-occlusion, fat embolism from infarcted marrow, or infection.
Pallor / scleral icterus~15–30%Chronic hemolysis: anemia (pallor) and unconjugated bilirubin (icterus, pigment gallstones).
Priapism<10% (males)Vaso-occlusion of penile venous outflow; ischemic and time-critical.
Focal neuro deficit<5%Large-vessel occlusion/stroke — a neurologic emergency needing urgent exchange transfusion.
Read the patternUncomplicated VOC is pain in the patient's usual pattern with stable vitals and clear lungs. The job at the bedside is to treat that pain hard while screening for the four things that turn a crisis lethal: acute chest syndrome, infection/sepsis, stroke, and splenic sequestration.
🪛

Imaging findings — what to order and the threshold to order it

Study / findingWhen it appears / order thresholdWhy
Chest X-ray — new infiltrate (often lower lobes, bilateral)Any respiratory symptom, hypoxia, fever, or chest/severe upper-back painDefines acute chest syndrome. Infiltrate may lag symptoms by 1–2 days — repeat if the first film is clean but suspicion is high.
CT pulmonary angiogramIf PE genuinely suspected (pleuritic pain, ↑A-a, risk factors)SCD is prothrombotic; but don't reflexively CT every crisis — ACS mimics PE and is far more common.
Transcranial Doppler (TCD)Screening ages 2–16 (HbSS/Sβ⁰), not acuteTime-averaged mean velocity ≥200 cm/s = high stroke risk → chronic transfusion (STOP trial).
MRI/MRA brainAny acute focal deficit or altered mentationDetects acute and silent infarcts; MRA maps large-vessel vasculopathy/moyamoya.
Plain film / MRI of hipChronic hip/shoulder pain, limpAvascular necrosis of the femoral/humeral head from repeated marrow infarction; MRI is earliest.
Abdominal ultrasoundRUQ pain, rising bilirubin, big spleenPigment gallstones (chronic hemolysis), hepatic/splenic sequestration.
Diffuse bilateral alveolar infiltrates. Severe acute chest syndrome looks the same radiographically — a new infiltrate plus a respiratory symptom or fever in an SCD patient defines ACS (illustrative bilateral-infiltrate film).
Image: van der Vaart et al., public domain (US CDC/EID), via Wikimedia Commons
Avascular (aseptic) necrosis of the femoral head — a chronic consequence of repeated bone/marrow vaso-occlusion; presents as deep hip/groin pain.

🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you (and what fools it)

LabWhat it means & why it moves
HemoglobinKnow the patient's baseline (often 6–9 in HbSS). A crisis alone doesn't drop Hb much — a fall of ≥2 g/dL below baseline means sequestration, aplastic crisis, hyperhemolysis, or bleeding, not "just pain." A rising Hb during ACS can worsen viscosity.
Reticulocyte countThe single most useful sorter. Baseline is high (brisk compensation). Low retic (<1–2%) with falling Hb = aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19). Very high retic with a big spleen = sequestration/hyperhemolysis.
LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobinMarkers of ongoing hemolysis — LDH and indirect bilirubin up, haptoglobin down. A sharp rise above the patient's usual signals a hyperhemolytic event.
WBCOften mildly elevated from marrow stress/inflammation, and higher WBC correlates with severity — but a left shift, bands, or a big jump demands a hunt for infection (asplenia). Don't attribute leukocytosis to the crisis alone.
Creatinine / BUNSCD nephropathy blunts baseline creatinine (hyperfiltration) — a "normal" value may hide real injury. NSAIDs, contrast and hypovolemia during a crisis can tip into AKI.
Oxygen saturation / A-a gradientNew hypoxia is an ACS alarm. Pulse oximetry can read imperfectly because HbS has altered O₂ affinity — trend it and get an ABG if the number and the patient disagree.
Type & screen (extended phenotype)Send early if transfusion is on the table. These patients alloimmunize easily, so give C/E/K-matched, HbS-negative units and watch for delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions.
Blood culturesDraw before antibiotics whenever febrile — functional asplenia means Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus, Salmonella osteomyelitis and Gram-negatives can be fulminant.
Howell–Jolly body (nuclear remnant, the dark inclusion) — a smear marker of the functional asplenia (autosplenectomy) that makes every fever an emergency.
Image: P.H.O. Mourão & M. Häggström, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Proliferative sickle retinopathy — peripheral "sea-fan" neovascularization from retinal vaso-occlusion; a reason for annual dilated eye exams.
Image: Linz & Scott, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
🩺 Clinic — disease-modifying therapy, prevention & keeping crises from happening
Assess

The outpatient picture

🔍

Who you're seeing in clinic

The clinic patient is between crises: chronic hemolytic anemia (fatigue, scleral icterus, flow murmur), a history of recurrent pain episodes, and the slow accrual of end-organ damage. Your leverage here is enormous — the drugs that prevent crises live in clinic, and consistent preventive care is the difference between a few pain days a year and a life shaped by the disease.

Anchor every visit on three questions: (1) How many crises / ACS episodes / hospital days since I last saw you? (drives disease-modifying therapy), (2) Are we screening the organs sickle cell silently damages? (brain, lung, kidney, eye, heart, hip), and (3) Are the preventable killers covered? (vaccines, penicillin in kids, a fever action plan).

Ask specifically about opioid use and a home pain plan. Many patients arrive at the ED already on chronic opioids; a written, patient-specific analgesia plan in the chart speeds effective ED dosing and reduces the friction and bias these patients routinely face.

Treat

Disease-modifying therapy — first-line → escalation

💊

Stopping crises before they start

1
First-line — Hydroxyurea (offer to essentially all HbSS/HbSβ⁰)
The one drug that changes the natural history. ASH 2020 recommends offering it regardless of crisis count.
▾
Hydroxyurea (a ribonucleotide-reductase inhibitor) reinduces fetal hemoglobin, and HbF can't join the HbS polymer — so red cells resist sickling. It also lowers the neutrophil and reticulocyte counts (less adhesion), raises MCV, and boosts NO. Net effect in the MSH trial: ~50% fewer painful crises, fewer ACS episodes, fewer transfusions.
DrugStartTitration → Target / MaxWhy it worksIf intolerant / alternative
Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) 15 mg/kg/day PO once daily (round to nearest 500 mg cap). Start 5–10 mg/kg/day if CKD. ↑ by 5 mg/kg/day every 8 weeks to the maximum tolerated dose — target mild myelosuppression (ANC ~2000–4000) and rising HbF. Max 35 mg/kg/day. ↑HbF → polymer can't form; ↓WBC/retic adhesion; ↑NO. Disease-modifying, with a mortality benefit. Cytopenias/GI intolerance → hold, resume lower. If truly not tolerated or inadequate → L-glutamine, crizanlizumab, or chronic transfusion (rungs 2–3).
Counsel on contraception (teratogenic), expect a benign rise in MCV as a marker of adherence, and check CBC + retic every 2 weeks during titration, then every 8–12 weeks. Benefits take 3–6 months — don't call it a failure early.
2
Add-on — L-glutamine and/or crizanlizumab
For breakthrough crises on maximal hydroxyurea, or when hydroxyurea isn't tolerated.
▾
DrugStart / DoseTitration → TargetWhy it worksIf allergic / caution
L-glutamine (Endari) 0.3 g/kg/dose PO twice daily, weight-banded. Fixed by weight: <30 kg = 5 g BID · 30–65 kg = 10 g BID · >65 kg = 15 g BID (max). No titration. Substrate for NAD synthesis → replenishes red-cell antioxidant capacity → less oxidative membrane injury and sickling/adhesion (~25% fewer crises). Well tolerated; mild GI/constipation. Can combine with hydroxyurea.
Crizanlizumab (Adakveo) 5 mg/kg IV at week 0 and week 2. Then 5 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks. Infuse over 30 min; watch for infusion reactions. Monoclonal antibody against P-selectin — blocks the adhesion step that nucleates the clog (SUSTAIN: fewer crises). Note the confirmatory STAND trial did not confirm benefit — EMA revoked approval (2023), though it remains FDA-approved in the US (≥16 y); weigh access, cost and evolving evidence.
Voxelotor (Oxbryta) — an HbS-polymerization inhibitor — was withdrawn from the worldwide market by Pfizer in September 2024 after post-marketing data showed an imbalance in vaso-occlusive crises and deaths. It is no longer a recommended therapy; do not start it, and transition any patient still taking it.
3
Transfusion program, gene therapy & transplant — the specialist tier
For stroke risk, refractory disease, or a shot at cure.
▾
  • Chronic (simple or exchange) transfusion program — first-line for primary stroke prevention (abnormal TCD ≥200 cm/s, STOP trial) and secondary stroke prevention; keep HbS <30%. Downside: iron overload → chelation.
  • Iron chelation for transfusional overload (ferritin persistently >1000 or elevated LIC): deferasirox (Jadenu film-coated) start 14 mg/kg/day, titrate by 3.5–7 mg/kg to max 28 mg/kg/day; alternatives deferoxamine SC/IV or deferiprone (watch agranulocytosis).
  • Gene therapy (FDA-approved Dec 2023, age ≥12 with recurrent VOCs): exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) — CRISPR editing of BCL11A to reactivate HbF — and lovotibeglogene autotemcel (Lyfgenia) — lentiviral anti-sickling β-globin (boxed warning for hematologic malignancy/AML). Both require myeloablative busulfan conditioning.
  • Allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplant — the only established cure; best results with an HLA-matched sibling donor, ideally in children before organ damage accrues.
Notice the shared logic: transfusion dilutes HbS, gene therapy manufactures anti-sickling hemoglobin (HbF or βA-T87Q), and transplant replaces the marrow — three routes to the same target the cascade demands: fewer sickle-prone cells.

Every-visit foundation therapy: folic acid 1 mg PO daily (supports the high red-cell turnover) and adherence support for the drugs above.

Comorbidities

How comorbidities change the plan

🔗

The company sickle cell keeps

Sickle cell disease is a whole-body vasculopathy, so its "comorbidities" are often its own end-organ damage. Each one bends both the risk of crisis and how you can safely treat it.

ComorbidityHow it interactsWhat changes in management
Asthma / reactive airwaysStrong, independent risk factor for acute chest syndrome and recurrent wheeze.Optimize controller therapy; treat wheeze aggressively during crises; low threshold for ACS workup.
Chronic kidney diseaseSickle nephropathy (hyperfiltration → albuminuria → CKD); masks true creatinine.ACE-I/ARB for albuminuria; avoid NSAIDs and contrast; dose-reduce hydroxyurea; watch K⁺.
Pulmonary hypertensionHemolysis-driven NO depletion; marks high mortality (TRV ≥2.5 m/s).Confirm with right-heart cath; optimize hydroxyurea/transfusion; refer to PH specialist.
Avascular necrosis (hip/shoulder)Repeated bone infarction → chronic non-crisis pain that opioids won't fix.PT, joint-preserving surgery, arthroplasty; separate this pain from acute VOC.
Iron overload (transfused)Cumulative transfusion iron → liver, heart, endocrine damage.Monitor ferritin/LIC/cardiac T2* MRI; chelate; consider exchange over simple transfusion to limit iron.
AlloimmunizationRepeated transfusion → antibodies → hard cross-match, delayed hemolytic reactions.Use extended (C/E/K) phenotype-matched, sickle-negative units; keep an antibody card.
PregnancyMore frequent crises, ACS, VTE, pre-eclampsia; hydroxyurea is teratogenic.Stop hydroxyurea preconception; co-manage with MFM; prophylactic/transfusion strategies individualized.
Leg ulcers, gallstones, priapismChronic hemolytic vasculopathy manifestations.Wound care/compression; cholecystectomy for symptomatic stones; urology for recurrent priapism.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in SCD: meperidine (normeperidine accumulates → seizures — never use it for VOC); NSAIDs in CKD/AKI or dehydration (nephrotoxic; ketorolac only short-term); excessive supplemental O₂ when not hypoxic (suppresses erythropoiesis and doesn't help); over-transfusion to Hb >10–11 (hyperviscosity → paradoxically more vaso-occlusion/stroke); cold IV fluids/environments (provoke sickling); and voxelotor (withdrawn 2024). Give iron only if proven deficient — most SCD anemia is hemolytic, not iron-deficient.

Prevent

Vaccines, prophylaxis & USPSTF A/B

🛡️

The preventable killers — cover them every visit

SCD-specific prevention (functional asplenia makes this life-or-death)

  • Penicillin prophylaxis in children: penicillin V 125 mg PO BID <3 y, 250 mg PO BID ages 3–5 y (PROPS trial ↓ pneumococcal sepsis); continue past 5 y if prior invasive pneumococcal disease or splenectomy.
  • Vaccinate against encapsulated organisms: pneumococcal (PCV15/20 then PPSV23), Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcal ACWY + B, plus annual influenza and COVID-19.
  • Fever action plan: any temp ≥38.5 °C → same-day evaluation, cultures, and empiric antibiotics — teach families this cold.
  • Hydroxyurea & folic acid as above; TCD, retinal, renal and PH screening as under Workup.

Relevant USPSTF Grade A & B recommendations

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AScreen all newborns for sickle cell diseaseUniversal US newborn screening — how most patients are identified
BDepression screening (chronic pain/illness carries high burden)All adults & adolescents, with follow-up systems
ATobacco cessation — ask + counsel + pharmacotherapyAll adults (smoking compounds pulmonary/vascular risk)
BFolic acid supplementationPeople who may become pregnant (and SCD needs it for turnover)
AScreen for HIV / HBV / HCVAdolescents & adults, especially if transfused historically
USPSTF has no sickle-cell-specific chronic-management A/B statement beyond newborn screening — the disease-specific prophylaxis (penicillin, vaccines, TCD) comes from NHLBI 2014 and ASH 2020, not USPSTF. Cover both sets.
Monitor

Titration & follow-up cadence

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Starting/titrating hydroxyurea: CBC + retic every 2 weeks (watch for excess myelosuppression); once stable, every 8–12 weeks with HbF%.
  • Every 8 weeks: assess for the +5 mg/kg step if ANC/platelets allow and crises persist.
  • Annually: TCD (ages 2–16), dilated retinal exam, urine albumin/creatinine, BMP; periodic echo (TRV) and hip imaging if symptomatic.
  • Chronically transfused: ferritin every ~3 months, cardiac T2*/LIC MRI to guide chelation, and red-cell antibody screen.
  • Track the outcome that matters: crises per year, ED/hospital days, ACS episodes — the trend tells you whether therapy is working.
Escalate

When to send to the ED / admit

🚑

Red flags — "don't manage this in clinic"

Fever ≥38.5 °C (sepsis until proven otherwise) · chest pain, dyspnea, or new hypoxia (acute chest syndrome) · any focal neuro deficit or severe headache (stroke) · an enlarging, tender spleen with pallor (sequestration) · Hb ≥2 g/dL below baseline or a low reticulocyte count (aplastic crisis) · priapism >4 hours · pain not controlled by the home regimen · signs of dehydration or AKI.
🛏️ Wards — the acute vaso-occlusive crisis admission
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & the "why now?" question

Many crises are treated aggressively in the ED/observation and resolve; admit when pain isn't controlled after adequate parenteral opioids, or when a complication is present or brewing. Always ask why this crisis, why now? — look for a trigger: infection, dehydration, cold exposure, hypoxia, stress, menses, alcohol, or missed hydroxyurea.

Admit for…Because…
Pain uncontrolled after 2–3 parenteral opioid dosesNeeds scheduled/PCA opioids and time.
Any acute chest syndrome (or new hypoxia/infiltrate)Can deteriorate fast; the leading cause of death.
Fever with ill appearance, or a focus of infectionAsplenia → fulminant sepsis risk.
Hb ≥2 g/dL below baseline, low retic, or enlarging spleenAplastic crisis / sequestration / hyperhemolysis.
Dehydration, vomiting, AKI, or unable to take oralsNeeds IV fluids and closer monitoring.
Priapism >4 h, neuro change, or pregnancy with a crisisEmergencies / higher-risk hosts.

Treat

Acute management — the pain ladder

💊

Treat pain fast, screen for complications relentlessly

Opioids and NSAIDs don't unclog the vessel — they control the ischemic pain while hydration/oxygen remove the trigger and the occlusion resolves. The evidence-based lever that changes outcome is speed and adequacy of analgesia: ASH 2020 recommends rapid (within 30–60 min of arrival) individualized opioid dosing with frequent reassessment.
1
First-line — rapid parenteral opioids (individualized)
Use the patient's own protocol if one exists; otherwise weight-based.
▾
DrugStart (opioid-naïve estimate)Titration → TargetWhy it worksIf allergic / caution
Morphine IV 0.1–0.15 mg/kg IV within 30–60 min of arrival. Reassess pain every 15–30 min; redose 25–50% of the initial dose until controlled, then transition to PCA or scheduled dosing. μ-opioid agonist — blunts nociceptive transmission from ischemic tissue. Does not treat sickling. Avoid in morphine allergy or significant renal failure (metabolite accumulation) → use hydromorphone.
Hydromorphone IV 0.015–0.02 mg/kg IV (≈ 0.5–1 mg) — preferred in renal impairment. Same reassess-and-redose cadence; convert to PCA once a dose requirement is clear. More potent μ-agonist, fewer active renal metabolites than morphine. Respiratory depression — monitor sedation/RR, have naloxone available.
PCA (patient-controlled analgesia) Start once dose need is established (e.g., hydromorphone 0.2 mg demand, lockout 6–10 min ± basal). Titrate demand/basal to comfort & safe sedation; reassess q shift. Steady analgesia, patient autonomy, fewer peaks/troughs. Basal rates raise apnea risk — monitor closely, especially with ACS.
Never use meperidine (pethidine) — its metabolite normeperidine accumulates and causes seizures, especially with the renal impairment common in SCD.
2
Add adjuncts & supportive care (opioid-sparing)
Layer these on from the start, not as an afterthought.
▾
AdjunctDoseRole / targetWhy it worksCaution
Ketorolac IV15–30 mg IV q6h (0.5 mg/kg, max 30) — limit to ≤5 days.Opioid-sparing anti-inflammatory.Blocks prostaglandin-mediated inflammatory pain from ischemia.Avoid in AKI/CKD, dehydration, GI bleed; renal-dose.
Acetaminophen650–1000 mg PO/IV q6h (≤3–4 g/day).Baseline multimodal analgesia.Central analgesic; safe opioid-sparing floor.Cap the dose in liver disease.
Incentive spirometry10 breaths q2h awake.ACS prevention.Keeps alveoli open; counters the splinting from chest/back pain that seeds atelectasis → ACS.—
IV fluids (isotonic)Correct deficit, then maintenance or below.Reverse the dehydration trigger.Lowers intracellular HbS concentration and viscosity — but excess causes pulmonary edema/ACS.Avoid over-hydration; warm the fluids.
OxygenTitrate to SpO₂ ≥95%.Only if hypoxic.Corrects the hypoxemic sickling trigger.Don't give routine O₂ if saturated — no benefit, suppresses erythropoiesis.
Warmth, non-pharmacologicWarm compresses, quiet room.Reduce sickling & distress.Cold provokes vasoconstriction/sickling.Avoid ice packs.
Do not transfuse an uncomplicated pain crisis. Transfusion has no role for pain alone; reserve it for ACS, stroke, symptomatic anemia, sequestration, aplastic crisis, or pre-op — see the ICU transfusion tool.
3
Escalate — complication-directed therapy
When the crisis is no longer "just pain."
▾
  • Acute chest syndrome: add empiric antibiotics (3rd-gen cephalosporin + macrolide), escalate O₂, bronchodilators if wheezing, and transfuse (simple vs exchange by severity — see ICU).
  • Fever/sepsis: cultures then prompt empiric antibiotics covering encapsulated organisms.
  • Stroke: emergent neuro-imaging and urgent exchange transfusion to HbS <30%.
  • Splenic sequestration: transfuse cautiously (autotransfusion on recovery); aplastic crisis: transfuse for symptomatic anemia, supportive care.
  • Priapism >4 h: urology — aspiration + intracavernosal phenylephrine; analgesia and hydration.
Monitor

What to trend each day

📈

Daily assessment targets

  • Pain scores & opioid requirement — is the trend down? Start weaning parenteral → oral as pain eases; begin a bowel regimen on day 1.
  • Respiratory status & SpO₂ — the ACS watch: new hypoxia, tachypnea, chest pain, or a falling saturation → repeat CXR and escalate.
  • Hemoglobin & reticulocytes — a drop of ≥2 g/dL from baseline changes the diagnosis (sequestration/aplastic/hyperhemolysis).
  • Temperature / WBC — new fever or leukocytosis with left shift → re-culture, reconsider infection/ACS.
  • Volume status & renal function — avoid both dehydration and fluid overload; watch creatinine if NSAIDs/contrast were used.
  • Incentive spirometry adherence — actually confirm it's being done.
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers (be concrete)

Transfer for: SpO₂ <90% on supplemental O₂ or a rising O₂ requirement; respiratory rate >30 / accessory-muscle use / rapidly progressing (multilobar) ACS; need for exchange transfusion; any acute neurologic deficit / stroke; hemodynamic instability or sepsis needing pressors; multiorgan dysfunction (rising creatinine/LFTs, encephalopathy — the sickle multiorgan-failure syndrome); or hemoglobin falling despite transfusion.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: pain controlled on the oral regimen for ≥12–24 h, able to hydrate and ambulate, no hypoxia and no evolving ACS, hemoglobin at/near baseline, and a clear opioid taper + follow-up plan (hematology within 1–2 weeks; confirm hydroxyurea adherence and refill).

Home

The overwhelming majority — pain controlled orally, reliable, with a written taper and hematology follow-up.

Home health

Occasionally for IV chelation teaching, wound (leg-ulcer) care, or infusion support.

SNF

Rare; older patients with deconditioning or new functional loss needing skilled nursing.

Acute rehab (IRF)

After a disabling stroke or major orthopedic surgery (e.g., hip arthroplasty for AVN) if ≥3 h therapy/day is tolerated.

LTAC

Prolonged critical illness — e.g., ventilator weaning after severe ACS/ARDS.

Palliative / hospice

Advanced end-organ disease (PH, chronic pain, organ failure) — comfort-focused symptom & goals-of-care support alongside disease care.
🫀 ICU — acute chest syndrome, transfusion strategy & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers & severity

🚨

When the crisis becomes critical

Sickle cell patients reach the unit for a short list of reasons — and acute chest syndrome tops it. Recognize severity early, because ACS can march from a little hypoxia to ARDS in under a day.

ICU indicationSeverity marker
Severe / progressive acute chest syndromeMultilobar infiltrates, SpO₂ <90% on O₂, falling PaO₂/FiO₂, rising work of breathing.
Acute ischemic stroke / neuro deteriorationAny focal deficit or altered mentation — needs emergent exchange transfusion.
Multiorgan failure syndromeAcute liver + kidney + neuro dysfunction with fever during a severe crisis.
Sepsis / shockHypotension, lactate elevation — asplenic host; pressor need.
Need for exchange transfusion / apheresisSevere ACS, stroke, MOF — target HbS <30%.
Acute chest syndrome is the leading cause of death and of ICU admission in SCD. New infiltrate + (fever OR chest pain OR hypoxia OR tachypnea/wheeze) = ACS — start treatment before it "declares."
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous SpO₂ + frequent ABG — track PaO₂/FiO₂; remember HbS can make pulse oximetry read imperfectly.
  • Large-bore / central access for exchange transfusion or apheresis; involve the blood bank early (extended phenotype-matched, sickle-negative units — cross-matching takes time in alloimmunized patients).
  • Serial Hb, HbS%, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin — follow response to transfusion and watch for hyperhemolysis/DHTR.
  • Renal & hepatic panels, lactate, coagulation — detect evolving multiorgan failure early.
  • Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring; low threshold for a repeat CXR as ACS evolves.
Support

Transfusion strategy — simple vs exchange

🩸

The central ICU decision in SCD

Transfusion is disease-directed here: it replaces sickle-prone HbS cells with normal HbA cells, cutting the HbS fraction so polymerization and vaso-occlusion stop. Simple (top-up) transfusion raises oxygen-carrying capacity when the patient is anemic; exchange transfusion (manual or automated apheresis) rapidly lowers HbS% without raising total Hb — essential when you must drop HbS but can't afford hyperviscosity.
Simple raises capacity; exchange lowers HbS% without raising viscosity. The ceiling of Hb ≤10 protects against hyperviscosity in both.
ScenarioStrategyTarget
Uncomplicated pain crisisNo transfusion—
Symptomatic anemia / aplastic / sequestrationSimpleHb ~9–10 (never >10–11)
Moderate ACS (hypoxia, anemic)SimpleImprove oxygenation; Hb ≤10
Severe / rapidly progressive ACSExchangeHbS <30% (<20% if intubated), Hb ≤10
Acute ischemic strokeExchange (urgent)HbS <30%
Multiorgan failure syndromeExchangeHbS <30%

Support

Pressors — if shock complicates the crisis

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Shock in SCD is usually septic (asplenic host) or hypovolemic (splenic/hepatic sequestration → treat with volume + transfusion). Manage it on standard sepsis principles — there is no sickle-specific pressor — while you culture, give broad antibiotics, and correct the anemia.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate to MAP ≥65)↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line for septic/distributive shock.
VasopressinV1 receptor0.03 units/min (fixed, add-on)↑SVR (catecholamine-sparing)Add to norepinephrine when MAP still low.
Epinephrineβ1 = α1 > β20.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVR, ↑HRSecond-line / refractory septic shock.
Dobutamineβ1 > β2 inotrope2.5–10 mcg/kg/min↑contractility, ↑COIf a cardiogenic component / low output.
Norepinephrine restores perfusion pressure with minimal tachycardia; keep the patient warm, well-oxygenated and euvolemic — the same measures that avoid perfusion collapse also avoid a fresh sickling trigger.
Airway

Respiratory support for ACS/ARDS

🌬️

From nasal O₂ to lung-protective ventilation

Escalate stepwise: supplemental O₂ → high-flow nasal cannula/NIV for hypoxemic respiratory failure → intubation when NIV fails or the patient tires. Keep transfusing to the HbS target in parallel — the definitive lung therapy for severe ACS is transfusion, not the ventilator. If ACS progresses to ARDS, ventilate lung-protectively.

Mode
AC/VC

Tidal volume

Aggressive incentive spirometry, adequate (not excessive) analgesia so the patient can breathe deeply, and early transfusion prevent most intubations. ECMO has been used successfully as a bridge in refractory ACS/ARDS.
Rescue

Advanced / rescue therapies

⚙️

When first-line isn't enough

  • Automated red-cell exchange (apheresis) — rapidly drives HbS <30% for severe ACS, stroke, or multiorgan failure without raising viscosity; the definitive rescue.
  • Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics maintained through septic/ACS courses (cephalosporin + macrolide, broaden for shock).
  • ECMO (veno-venous) as a bridge in refractory ACS/ARDS.
  • Multiorgan failure syndrome: aggressive exchange transfusion is the key intervention; support each failing organ (CRRT, etc.).
  • Priapism refractory to aspiration/phenylephrine → urologic shunt; stroke → stroke team + exchange (thrombolysis is generally not used for sickle-related occlusion).
Avoid the classic traps even in the unit: no meperidine, no routine O₂ if saturated, no over-transfusion above Hb 10–11, no cold fluids, and no NSAIDs in AKI.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: oxygenation is improving on ≤ low-flow O₂ (SpO₂ ≥92–95%) with a stable/clearing CXR, off vasopressors with stable hemodynamics, HbS at target after exchange and hemoglobin stable, neuro status stable/improving, and pain manageable on a floor-appropriate regimen. Not yet if the O₂ requirement is still climbing, ACS is multilobar and progressing, or organ dysfunction hasn't turned the corner.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The dozen things that actually change outcomes at the bedside

  1. Believe the pain and treat it fast. Give an opioid within 30–60 min of arrival and reassess every 15–30 min. Sickle patients are systematically under-treated because of bias — the crisis is invisible on every test you can run.
  2. Fever in SCD is an emergency, not a symptom of the crisis. Functional asplenia makes encapsulated-organism sepsis fulminant — culture and give empiric antibiotics; never blame a fever on "just the pain."
  3. Do not transfuse an uncomplicated pain crisis. Transfusion helps ACS, stroke, symptomatic anemia, sequestration and aplastic crisis — not pain alone.
  4. Never give meperidine. Normeperidine accumulates (worse in renal impairment) and causes seizures.
  5. Incentive spirometry, 10 breaths q2h, is the cheapest ACS-prevention order you can write — chest/back pain makes patients splint and atelectatic, and atelectasis seeds acute chest syndrome.
  6. Oxygen only if hypoxic. Routine O₂ in a saturated patient doesn't help and suppresses reticulocytosis.
  7. Don't over-hydrate. Give maintenance or slightly below — excess fluid drives pulmonary edema and ACS.
  8. Keep total Hb ≤10–11 g/dL. Over-transfusion causes hyperviscosity and can paradoxically cause more vaso-occlusion and stroke; exchange lowers HbS without raising viscosity.
  9. The reticulocyte count sorts a sudden drop in Hb: low retic → aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19); high retic + big spleen → sequestration or hyperhemolysis.
  10. Offer hydroxyurea to essentially every HbSS/HbSβ⁰ patient regardless of how many crises they've had (ASH 2020). A rising MCV confirms adherence; benefits take 3–6 months.
  11. A crisis that feels "different" from the patient's usual pattern should trigger a hunt for a complication — ACS, infection, avascular necrosis, cord compression, or PE.
  12. Voxelotor (Oxbryta) is off the market (withdrawn September 2024) — don't start it, and give extended phenotype-matched, sickle-negative units to limit alloimmunization; a post-transfusion Hb drop with pain may be hyperhemolysis, not a new crisis.
